claim: Oxidized phospholipids are produced by peroxidation of cell membrane or lipoprotein phospholipids, usually during inflammation or senescence.
source: Oxidized phospholipids (oxPLs) are produced by peroxidation of cell membrane or lipoprotein phospholipids, usually during inflammation or senescence (Bochkov et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bochkov et al., 2010

claim: Oxidized phospholipids can be recognized by many receptors in the innate immune system.
source: They can be recognized by many receptors in the innate immune system, often with significant consequences (Bochkov et al., 2017; Bochkov et al., 2010; Erridge et al., 2008; Hazen, 2008; Matt et al., 2015; Mauerhofer et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: PGPC and POVPC are oxidation products of PAPC.
source: For example, 1-palmitoyl-2-glutaroyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphocholine (PGPC) and 1-palmitoyl-2-(5-oxovaleroyl)-sn-glycero-3-phosphocholine (POVPC), two important oxidation products of 1-palmitoyl-2-arachidonoyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphocholine (PAPC), can activate acid sphingomyelinase to produce ceramide that then induces cell death of smooth muscle cells and macrophages (Greig et al., 2012; Loidl et al., 2003; Stemmer et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Greig et al., 2012; Loidl et al., 2003; Stemmer et al., 2012

claim: PGPC and POVPC can activate acid sphingomyelinase to produce ceramide that induces cell death of smooth muscle cells and macrophages.
source: For example, 1-palmitoyl-2-glutaroyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphocholine (PGPC) and 1-palmitoyl-2-(5-oxovaleroyl)-sn-glycero-3-phosphocholine (POVPC), two important oxidation products of 1-palmitoyl-2-arachidonoyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphocholine (PAPC), can activate acid sphingomyelinase to produce ceramide that then induces cell death of smooth muscle cells and macrophages (Greig et al., 2012; Loidl et al., 2003; Stemmer et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Greig et al., 2012; Loidl et al., 2003; Stemmer et al., 2012

claim: OxPLs may trigger apoptosis in ER-stressed macrophages in a CD36-TLR2 dependent manner.
source: In endoplasmic reticulum-stressed macrophages, oxPLs may also trigger apoptosis in a CD36-TLR2 dependent manner (Seimon et al., 2010)
evidence: Supported by citation to Seimon et al., 2010

claim: PGPC and POVPC may induce IL-1β release from macrophages or dendritic cells that have been primed by LPS or other TLR agonists in a NLRP3 and caspase 1/11-dependent manner.
source: For example, PGPC and POVPC may induce IL-1β release from macrophages or dendritic cells that have been primed by lipopolysaccharide (LPS) or other TLR agonists in a NLRP3 and caspase 1/11-dependent manner (Yeon et al., 2017; Zanoni et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Yeon et al., 2017; Zanoni et al., 2017

claim: PGPC and POVPC can induce IL-1β release without inducing pyroptosis.
source: Zanoni et al. have found that PGPC and POVPC, unlike other inflammasome activators, can induce IL-1β release without inducing pyroptosis (Evavold et al., 2018; Hagar et al., 2013; Kayagaki et al., 2011; Kayagaki et al., 2013; Mangan et al., 2018; Shi et al., 2015; Shi et al., 2014; Zanoni et al., 2016; Zanoni et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: CD14 captures and internalizes PGPC and POVPC, and this mode of cell entry is required for these oxPLs to induce macrophages to release IL-1β.
source: Building on evidence that cell-surface CD14 can bind and internalize glycerophosphoinositides (Wang et al., 1998; Wang and Munford, 1999), Zanoni et al. found that CD14 captures and internalizes PGPC and POVPC and showed that this mode of cell entry is required for these oxPLs to induce macrophages to release IL-1β (Zanoni et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wang et al., 1998; Wang and Munford, 1999; Zanoni et al., 2017

claim: AOAH is a highly conserved animal lipase expressed in phagocytes, NK cells, type 1 innate lymphoid cells, and renal proximal tubule cells.
source: Acyloxyacyl hydrolase (AOAH), a highly conserved animal lipase, is expressed in phagocytes, including macrophages, microglia, dendritic cells and neutrophils, and also in NK cells, type 1 innate lymphoid cells, and renal proximal tubule cells (Munford et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Munford et al., 2020

claim: AOAH transforms bacterial LPS by cleaving ester bonds that attach secondary fatty acyl chains to primary hydroxyacyl chains in the lipid A moiety, converting a potent stimulus to a competitive inhibitor.
source: AOAH transforms bacterial LPS by cleaving the ester bonds that attach the secondary ('piggyback') fatty acyl chains to the primary (glucosamine-bound) hydroxyacyl chains in the lipid A moiety, converting a potent stimulus to a competitive inhibitor (Munford et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Munford et al., 2020

claim: AOAH can remove fatty acyl chains from the sn-1 and sn-2 positions of many glycero(phospho)lipids and be an acyl transferase.
source: In addition, AOAH can remove fatty acyl chains from the sn-1 and sn-2 positions of many glycero (phospho) lipids and be an acyl transferase (Gorelik et al., 2018; Munford and Hunter, 1992; Staab et al., 1994).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gorelik et al., 2018; Munford and Hunter, 1992; Staab et al., 1994

claim: 5–12.5 μg/ml PGPC or POVPC and 12.5 μg/ml oxPAPC induced significant cell death in mouse resident peritoneal macrophages with or without Pam3 priming.
source: We found that 5–12.5 μg/ml (8–21 μM) PGPC or POVPC and 12.5 μg/ml oxPAPC could induce significant cell death with or without Pam3 priming, whereas 12.5 μg/ml (16 μM) non-oxidized PAPC was inactive (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A

claim: Non-oxidized PAPC did not induce cell death in mouse resident peritoneal macrophages.
source: We found that 5–12.5 μg/ml (8–21 μM) PGPC or POVPC and 12.5 μg/ml oxPAPC could induce significant cell death with or without Pam3 priming, whereas 12.5 μg/ml (16 μM) non-oxidized PAPC was inactive (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A

claim: PGPC- and POVPC-induced IL-1β secretion occurred only in Pam3-primed cells and was dose-dependent.
source: PGPC- and POVPC-induced IL-1β secretion occurred only in Pam3-primed cells and was dose-dependent (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B

claim: Non-oxidized PAPC did not induce IL-1β release by primed cells.
source: Non-oxidized PAPC did not induce IL-1β release by primed cells (Figure 1B), in agreement with previous findings that only oxidized PLs activate the inflammasome (Zanoni et al., 2016; Zanoni et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 1B and citations to Zanoni et al., 2016; Zanoni et al., 2017

claim: Mature IL-1β (p17) appeared only after Pam3-primed macrophages had been treated with either PGPC or POVPC.
source: Mature IL-1β (p17) appeared only after Pam3-primed macrophages had been treated with either PGPC or POVPC (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D

claim: Caspase 1 inhibitor VX-765, caspase 8 inhibitor Z-IETD-FMK, NLPR3 inhibitor MCC950, and pan-caspase inhibitor Z-VAD-FMK significantly reduced IL-1β release and caspase 1 processing in primed macrophages but did not prevent oxPL-induced cell death.
source: We found that caspase 1 inhibitor VX-765, caspase 8 inhibitor Z-IETD-FMK, NLPR3 inhibitor MCC950, and pan-caspase inhibitor Z-VAD-FMK significantly reduced IL-1β release and caspase 1 processing in primed macrophages but did not prevent oxPL-induced cell death, demonstrating that oxPL-induced cell death does not require inflammasome activation (Stemmer et al., 2012; Figure 1E and F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 1E and F and citation to Stemmer et al., 2012

claim: OxPL-induced cell death does not require inflammasome activation.
source: We found that caspase 1 inhibitor VX-765, caspase 8 inhibitor Z-IETD-FMK, NLPR3 inhibitor MCC950, and pan-caspase inhibitor Z-VAD-FMK significantly reduced IL-1β release and caspase 1 processing in primed macrophages but did not prevent oxPL-induced cell death, demonstrating that oxPL-induced cell death does not require inflammasome activation (Stemmer et al., 2012; Figure 1E and F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 1E and F and citation to Stemmer et al., 2012

claim: Caspase 11 is not required for PGPC-induced IL-1β release from peritoneal macrophages that had been primed.
source: In contrast, we found that caspase 11 is not required for PGPC-induced IL-1β release from peritoneal macrophages that had been primed (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: AOAH removed the sn-2 and sn-1 acyl chains from both PGPC and POVPC.
source: Analysis using LC-MS showed that AOAH could remove the sn-2 oxidized fatty acyl chain and sn-1 palmitate from both PGPC and POVPC (Figure 2A and B)
evidence: Supported by LC-MS analysis data shown in Figure 2A and B

claim: AOAH preferentially removes the sn-2 moiety from PGPC and POVPC.
source: the sn-2 moiety was removed preferentially, in keeping with the enzyme's preference for removing shorter acyl chains from glycerolipids (Erwin and Munford, 1990; Gorelik et al., 2018; Munford and Hunter, 1992).
evidence: Supported by citations to Erwin and Munford, 1990; Gorelik et al., 2018; Munford and Hunter, 1992

claim: PGPC or POVPC treated with AOAH had greatly reduced ability to induce cell death in Pam3-primed macrophages.
source: PGPC or POVPC treated with AOAH (dPGPC or dPOVPC) had greatly reduced ability to induce cell death (Figure 2C and D)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C and D

claim: PGPC or POVPC treated with AOAH had greatly reduced ability to induce IL-1β release in Pam3-primed macrophages.
source: PGPC or POVPC treated with AOAH (dPGPC or dPOVPC) had greatly reduced ability to induce cell death (Figure 2C and D) and IL-1β release (Figure 2E and F) in Pam3-primed macrophages
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E and F

claim: When AOAH released the sn-2 oxidized acyl chains from PGPC or POVPC, the major product was LPC.
source: When AOAH released the sn-2 oxidized acyl chains from PGPC or POVPC, the major product was LPC (Figure 2A and B)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and B

claim: AOAH released palmitate from LPC.
source: When we incubated pure LPC with rhAOAH, we again found that palmitate was released (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A

claim: LPC induced cell death and IL-1β release by macrophages.
source: In agreement with previous reports that LPC can be inflammatory and induce IL-1β release (Li et al., 2016; Liu-Wu et al., 1998; Vladykovskaya et al., 2011), we found that LPC induced cell death and IL-1β release by macrophages
evidence: Supported by experimental data and citations to Li et al., 2016; Liu-Wu et al., 1998; Vladykovskaya et al., 2011

claim: LPC induced IL-1β release in a caspase 1, caspase 8, and NLRP3-dependent manner in primed macrophages.
source: as was observed with PGPC, LPC induced IL-1β release in a caspase 1, caspase 8, and NLRP3-dependent manner in primed macrophages, while inflammasome activation was not required for LPC-induced cell death (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B and C

claim: Inflammasome activation was not required for LPC-induced cell death.
source: as was observed with PGPC, LPC induced IL-1β release in a caspase 1, caspase 8, and NLRP3-dependent manner in primed macrophages, while inflammasome activation was not required for LPC-induced cell death (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B and C

claim: AOAH treatment partially diminished LPC bioactivities, including a major reduction in IL-1β release.
source: AOAH treatment partially diminished these bioactivities, including a major reduction in IL-1β release (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D

claim: In response to LPC, Pam3-primed Aoah-/- macrophages released more caspase 1 (p20) than did primed Aoah+/+ macrophages.
source: In response to LPC, Pam3-primed Aoah-/- macrophages released more caspase 1 (p20) than did primed Aoah+/+ macrophages (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E

claim: After Pam3 priming, PGPC or POVPC treatment led to more cell death in Aoah-/- macrophages than in Aoah+/+ controls.
source: After Pam3 priming, PGPC or POVPC treatment led to more cell death (Figure 4A) and more IL-1β release in Aoah-/- macrophages than in Aoah+/+ controls (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A

claim: After Pam3 priming, PGPC or POVPC treatment led to more IL-1β release in Aoah-/- macrophages than in Aoah+/+ controls.
source: After Pam3 priming, PGPC or POVPC treatment led to more cell death (Figure 4A) and more IL-1β release in Aoah-/- macrophages than in Aoah+/+ controls (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B

claim: AOAH does not regulate IL-6 secretion in response to Pam3 stimulation with or without oxPLs.
source: Although AOAH can deacylate synthetic lipopeptides, including Pam3 (Gorelik et al., 2018), AOAH did not regulate IL-6 secretion in response to Pam3 stimulation with or without oxPLs (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C and citation to Gorelik et al., 2018

claim: OxPLs induced significantly greater caspase 1 processing in Pam3-primed Aoah-/- macrophages than in Aoah+/+ macrophages.
source: In addition, we found that oxPLs induced significantly greater caspase 1 processing in Pam3-primed Aoah-/- macrophages, confirming that AOAH diminishes oxPL-induced inflammasome activation (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D

claim: After CpG-primed macrophages were treated with PGPC, more cell death and IL-1β release were found in Aoah-/- macrophages than in Aoah+/+ controls.
source: After CpG-primed macrophages were treated with PGPC, more cell death and IL-1β release were again found in Aoah-/- macrophages than in Aoah+/+ controls (Figure 4E), confirming that AOAH regulates the bioactivities of oxPLs.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E

claim: When PGPC or POVPC was delivered into the cell cytosol using DOTAP, primed Aoah+/+ and Aoah-/- macrophages released similar amounts of IL-1β.
source: When we delivered PGPC or POVPC into the cell cytosol using N-[1-(2,3-dioleoyloxy)propyl]-N,N,N-trimethylammonium methyl-sulfate (DOTAP), bypassing CD14 and endosomes (Zanoni et al., 2017), primed Aoah+/+ and Aoah-/- macrophages released similar amounts of IL-1β (Figure 4F)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4F and citation to Zanoni et al., 2017

claim: AOAH localizes in acidic cellular vesicles instead of cytosol.
source: in keeping with previous findings that AOAH localizes in acidic cellular vesicles instead of cytosol (Luchi and Munford, 1993; Munford and Hunter, 1992; Staab et al., 1994).
evidence: Supported by citations to Luchi and Munford, 1993; Munford and Hunter, 1992; Staab et al., 1994

claim: AOAH did not alter cytosolic LPS-induced IL-1β release.
source: In addition, AOAH did not alter cytosolic LPS-induced IL-1β release (Figure 4H; Shi et al., 2014; Zanoni et al., 2016)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4H and citations to Shi et al., 2014; Zanoni et al., 2016

claim: AOAH did not modulate ATP-induced inflammasome activation or IL-1β release in Pam3-primed macrophages.
source: or modulate ATP-induced inflammasome activation or IL-1β release in Pam3-primed macrophages (Figure 4I), evidence that AOAH does not prevent inflammasome activation per se.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4I

claim: OxPL internalization via CD14-induced endocytosis may allow AOAH to deacylate oxPLs before they activate the inflammasome.
source: These results suggest that oxPL internalization via CD14-induced endocytosis may allow AOAH, which is found in endolysosomes (Luchi and Munford, 1993; Staab et al., 1994), to deacylate oxPLs before they activate the inflammasome.
evidence: Supported by inference from experimental results and citations to Luchi and Munford, 1993; Staab et al., 1994

claim: OxPLs induced AOAH expression in alveolar macrophages by seven-fold in vivo.
source: We found that, unlike LPS, which stimulated AOAH mRNA expression in AMs by 100-fold in vivo (Zou et al., 2017), oxPLs induced AOAH expression by only seven-fold (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A and citation to Zou et al., 2017

claim: OxPLs reduced LPS-induced Aoah expression by alveolar macrophages.
source: Moreover, oxPLs reduced LPS-induced Aoah expression by AMs, suggesting that oxPLs may act as partial agonists to induce AOAH expression (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A

claim: Aoah-/- mice that received both LPS and oxPLs had more BALF protein and more neutrophils in their BALF than did identically treated Aoah+/+ mice.
source: Whereas Aoah+/+ and Aoah-/- mice had similar levels of protein in their bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) (reflecting alveolar leakage) 18 hr after either LPS or the oxPLs were introduced, Aoah-/- mice that received both LPS and oxPLs had more BALF protein and more neutrophils in their BALF at this time than did identically treated Aoah+/+ mice (Figure 5B and C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B and C

claim: After oxPLs were instilled, Aoah-/- mice had more monocytes-macrophages in their airspaces than did Aoah+/+ mice.
source: Notably, after oxPLs were instilled, Aoah-/- mice had more monocytes-macrophages in their airspaces than did Aoah+/+ mice (Figure 5C), suggesting that AOAH may regulate oxPL-induced inflammation.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C

claim: After LPS and oxPL instillation, both inflammatory and anti-inflammatory cytokine mRNA were more abundant in Aoah-/- mouse lungs than in Aoah+/+ mouse lungs.
source: After LPS and oxPL instillation, both inflammatory (IL-6, TNF-α, IL-1β, MCP-1) and anti-inflammatory (IL-10) cytokine mRNA were more abundant in Aoah-/- mouse lungs (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D

claim: The BALF from Aoah-/- mice contained more IL-6, TNF-α, and IL-1β than that from Aoah+/+ mice after LPS and oxPL instillation.
source: The BALF from Aoah-/- mouse contained more IL-6, TNF-α, and IL-1β than that from Aoah+/+ mice (Figure 5E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E

claim: Following instillation of S. pneumoniae plus oxPLs, Aoah-/- mice had greater leukocyte infiltration in their airspaces and more pulmonary IL-6, MCP-1, and KC mRNA than did Aoah+/+ mice.
source: Following instillation of S. pneumoniae plus oxPLs, we found that Aoah-/- mice had greater leukocyte infiltration in their airspaces and more pulmonary IL-6, MCP-1, and KC mRNA than did Aoah+/+ mice, providing further evidence that AOAH can act on oxPLs to ameliorate lung inflammation (Figure 5F and G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5F and G

claim: When both HCl and oxPLs were instilled, Aoah-/- mice had much more alveolar barrier damage and lung inflammation than did Aoah+/+ mice.
source: When both HCl and oxPLs were instilled, in contrast, Aoah-/- mice had much more alveolar barrier damage and lung inflammation than did Aoah+/+ mice (Figure 6A–D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A–D

claim: Transgenic mice that express high levels of AOAH had reduced airway inflammation after instillation of HCl plus oxPLs.
source: In addition, the transgenic mice that express high levels of AOAH (Ojogun et al., 2009) had reduced airway inflammation after instillation of HCl plus oxPLs (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1 and citation to Ojogun et al., 2009

claim: More E06-binding activity was detected in BALF from Aoah-/- mice than from Aoah+/+ mice after HCl and oxPL instillation.
source: We detected more E06-binding activity in BALF from Aoah-/- mice, suggesting that Aoah-/- mice were less able to degrade oxPLs in their airways (Figure 6E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E

claim: BALF from HCl- and oxPL-instilled Aoah-/- mice induced significantly more IL-1β production than did BALF from identically treated Aoah+/+ mice.
source: We used BALF to stimulate Pam3-primed macrophages and found that BALF from HCl- and oxPL-instilled Aoah-/- mice induced significantly more IL-1β production than did BALF from identically treated Aoah+/+ mice (Figure 6F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6F

claim: Pre-incubation with E06 Ab diminished the ability of BALF from Aoah-/- mice to induce IL-1β production.
source: Pre-incubation with E06 Ab diminished the ability of BALF from Aoah-/- mice to induce IL-1β production (Figure 6F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6F

claim: HCl-instilled and ventilated Aoah-/- mice had elevated BALF protein.
source: The HCl-instilled and ventilated Aoah-/- mice had elevated BALF protein, which was similar to the damage induced by HCl plus oxPLs but less than that induced by LPS and oxPLs (Figure 7A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A

claim: Ventilated Aoah-/- mice had more neutrophils and IL-6 in their airspaces as well as higher levels of lung inflammation than did Aoah+/+ control mice, especially when the mice had been instilled with HCl.
source: The ventilated Aoah-/- mice had more neutrophils and IL-6 in their airspaces as well as higher levels of lung inflammation than did Aoah+/+ control mice (Figure 7B–D), especially when the mice had been instilled with HCl.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B–D

claim: HCl-instilled, ventilated Aoah-/- mouse lungs had more leukocyte infiltration and alveolar barrier thickening than did control mouse lungs.
source: Histological study showed that HCl-instilled, ventilated Aoah-/- mouse lungs had more leukocyte infiltration and alveolar barrier thickening than did control mouse lungs (Figure 7E).
evidence: Supported by histological data shown in Figure 7E

claim: BALF from ventilated Aoah-/- mice bound more E06 antibody than did BALF from Aoah+/+ mice.
source: BALF from Aoah-/- mice not only bound more E06 antibody than did BALF from Aoah+/+ mice (Figure 7F)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7F

claim: BALF from ventilated Aoah-/- mice had greater ability to induce IL-1β release from Pam3-primed macrophages than BALF from Aoah+/+ mice.
source: but it also had greater ability to induce IL-1β release from Pam3-primed macrophages (Figure 7G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7G

claim: E06 partially inhibited the ability of BALF from ventilated Aoah-/- mice to induce IL-1β release from Pam3-primed macrophages.
source: This activity was partially inhibited by E06 (Figure 7G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7G

claim: Plasma platelet-activating factor acetyl hydrolase (PAF-AH) and intracellular PAF-AH II cleave sn-2 oxidized acyl chains from PGPC and POVPC.
source: Plasma platelet-activating factor acetyl hydrolase (PAF-AH) and intracellular PAF-AH II, which cleave sn-2 oxidized acyl chains from PGPC and POVPC, are GDSL lipases that have structural similarity to AOAH
evidence: Stated as established knowledge in the discussion

claim: PAF-AH and intracellular PAF-AH II are GDSL lipases that have structural similarity to AOAH.
source: Plasma platelet-activating factor acetyl hydrolase (PAF-AH) and intracellular PAF-AH II, which cleave sn-2 oxidized acyl chains from PGPC and POVPC, are GDSL lipases that have structural similarity to AOAH
evidence: Stated as established knowledge in the discussion

claim: AOAH-deacylated (tetraacyl) LPS has greatly reduced stimulatory potency and can inhibit LPS signaling by competing with LPS for binding to LPS-binding protein, soluble and membrane CD14, and MD-2.
source: AOAH-deacylated (tetraacyl) LPS has greatly reduced stimulatory potency and can inhibit LPS signaling by competing with LPS for binding to LPS-binding protein, soluble and membrane CD14, and MD-2 (Erwin and Munford, 1990; Kitchens et al., 1992; Munford and Hall, 1986; Munford and Hall, 1989).
evidence: Supported by citations to Erwin and Munford, 1990; Kitchens et al., 1992; Munford and Hall, 1986; Munford and Hall, 1989

claim: AOAH plays a significant role in inactivating both exogenously administered LPS and LPS derived from intestinal commensal Gram-negative bacteria.
source: Subsequent studies have found that AOAH plays a significant role in inactivating both exogenously administered LPS and LPS derived from intestinal commensal Gram-negative bacteria (Han et al., 2021; Lu et al., 2013; Lu et al., 2008; Lu et al., 2005; Qian et al., 2018; Shao et al., 2011; Shao et al., 2007; Zou et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Han et al., 2021; Lu et al., 2013; Lu et al., 2008; Lu et al., 2005; Qian et al., 2018; Shao et al., 2011; Shao et al., 2007; Zou et al., 2017

claim: AOAH does not prevent acute responses to LPS.
source: In previous studies, we found that AOAH does not prevent acute responses to LPS.
evidence: Stated based on previous studies by the authors

claim: AOAH modulates the late, or longer-lasting, responses to LPS stimulation.
source: Instead, the enzyme modulates the late, or longer-lasting, responses to LPS stimulation (Lu et al., 2008; Lu et al., 2005; Shao et al., 2007; Zou et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lu et al., 2008; Lu et al., 2005; Shao et al., 2007; Zou et al., 2017

claim: Aoah+/+ and Aoah-/- mice had similar degrees of lung injury 24 hr after LPS was instilled i.n., while on day 4, Aoah-/- mice showed delayed resolution of pulmonary inflammation.
source: Aoah+/+ and Aoah-/- mice had similar degrees of lung injury 24 hr after LPS was instilled i.n., while on day 4, Aoah-/- mice showed delayed resolution of pulmonary inflammation (Zou et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zou et al., 2017

claim: By inactivating oxPLs in endolysosomes, AOAH prevents oxPL leakage into the cytosol and endolysosomal damage, diminishing inflammasome activation.
source: By inactivating oxPLs in endolysosomes, AOAH prevents oxPL leakage into the cytosol and endolysosomal damage, diminishing inflammasome activation (Figure 8).
evidence: Supported by inference from experimental results and illustrated in Figure 8

claim: Endolysosomal AOAH cannot deacylate LPS before it is sensed by TLR4.
source: Thus, while endolysosomal AOAH cannot deacylate LPS before it is sensed by TLR4, the enzyme may act on oxPLs before they activate the inflammasome.
evidence: Inferred from the location of AOAH and the mechanism of LPS sensing

claim: Low concentrations of oxPLs have usually induced protective effects while high concentrations have been stimulatory/toxic.
source: Low concentrations of oxPLs have usually induced protective effects while high concentrations have been stimulatory/toxic (Mauerhofer et al., 2016; Muri et al., 2020; Oskolkova et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Mauerhofer et al., 2016; Muri et al., 2020; Oskolkova et al., 2010

claim: CD14 can transfer both LPS and oxPLs into endosomes.
source: It has been intriguing that CD14 can transfer both LPS and oxPLs into endosomes (Kitchens and Munford, 1998; Zanoni et al., 2017)
evidence: Supported by citations to Kitchens and Munford, 1998; Zanoni et al., 2017

claim: TLR4 and caspase 11 can recognize both oxPLs and LPS.
source: and that TLR4 and caspase 11 can recognize both oxPLs and LPS (Hagar et al., 2013; Imai et al., 2008; Kayagaki et al., 2011; Kayagaki et al., 2013; Shi et al., 2014; Zanoni et al., 2016)
evidence: Supported by citations to Hagar et al., 2013; Imai et al., 2008; Kayagaki et al., 2011; Kayagaki et al., 2013; Shi et al., 2014; Zanoni et al., 2016

claim: AOAH can inactivate both LPS and oxPLs and prevent them from inducing inflammasome activation.
source: here we show that the same lipase can inactivate both of these agonists and prevent them from inducing inflammasome activation.
evidence: Supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript
